doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
title: Ring-a-Ding-Ding! and Sinatra's arrangers and soloists
summary: Mandel discusses writing Sinatra's first Reprise album, how his jazz-minded approach differed from Nelson Riddle and Billy May.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: Which was the very first record that Sinatra did for Reprise.
Yeah, which was his company at the time.
Was that the very first Reprise record?
Well in terms of the people…
[laughs] Although in a sense you were because, say Nelson Riddle and Billy May and Gordon Jenkins had been doing his writing.
Oh, I’d followed all those great arrangers…
Yeah, I’ve referred to that, to Ring-a-Ding-Ding! half facetiously as Sinatra's bebop record and I'm exaggerating for effect but my point in that is…
I didn’t write any bebop in it.
I was by then that was like ten years after I was writing those bebop arrangements for Artie Shaw and people like that, I didn't really write like that anymore if you’d noticed.
I don't mind the way I wrote then, it's just that my head changed somewhat during those ten years. I got much more basic in terms of swing.
Although it's very subtle but I get it, like for example Nelson Riddle came out of the swing era.
Much more so than I did.
Although we were both in bands at the same time.
There’s a very subtle but different flavor in what you wrote for Sinatra but at the same time I mean it's totally appropriate and he's totally comfortable with it.
But there’s just a different flavor just because of your orientation that the fact that you came on the scene a little bit later.

Well I was much more of a jazz arranger than Nelson was too, whereas you can’t say that of Billy, Billy was always this free loose swinging wonderful arranger who started with Charlie Barnet. You know which was one of the great white swing bands, truly and very undervalued from a historical perspective.
Like for example on Ring-a-Ding-Ding!, just some of the soloist you use and the way you use them, like say with Don Fagerquist…
Yeah or Joe Maini or some… yeah.
Yeah, who was the lead alto player on that?
It was Joe? I was wondering whether it…
The best and I've never been able to replace him.
